Reflections: How Perth County sweated through the 1921 heat wave
Despite having quite a mild autumn this year, the scorching summer heat waves we have become accustomed to in this part of Ontario are not currently front and centre of people’s minds.
Some of us are lucky enough to have the modern convenience of air-conditioning in our homes while others are not so fortunate. Historically, people were certainly not able to simply turn on their air-conditioning to cool down their houses, which prompts the question: How did people cope with heat waves 100 years ago before window AC units became more common in North American houses in the 1950s? Taking a look back at one particularly troublesome heat wave in Perth County in 1921, newspapers provided details on how residents were coping with the sweltering temperatures.
It began on June 24 of that year. The entire province of Ontario was hit with a wall of heat unlike anything people living at the time had experienced before. Cities in particular were really feeling the heat, with soaring temperatures breaking records at the time. Since then, we have broken those temperature records again and again during our own contemporary summer heat waves, but at that time, it was a shock for Ontarians and Perth County wasn’t spared. The thermometer climbed to 34.4 C in Stratford on July 2. In the northern part of the county, residents of Listowel were sweating in 33 C heat. The heat wave lasted around three weeks before there was a break in the 30+ C weather. The temperature was notable enough to make the front page of several newspapers throughout Perth County. Below are some snippets from those articles:
“The popular greeting these days seems to be: ‘Isn’t it hot?’, and for once everyone has the right answer: ‘It is.’ In fact, it is getting hotter. Today at noon, the official observer, Mr. Alex Abraham, reported the temperature as 95 F in the shade. . . . The official readings are all mean temperature and, while they indicate great heat, they give no idea of what the heat, directly in the rays of the sun, would be. This much is assured that in the sun the heat would be from five to 10 degrees hotter than in the shade…
“One local church, Knox, held the evening service in the basement, thereby gaining some coolness. In another local church two men were brave enough to cast convention to the winds and take off their coats. They were in the front row, but the example wasn’t followed, the rest of the men in the congregation preferred to sit and suffer.
“One peculiar feature of the hot weather is the number of odd-looking outfits around the streets. That convict-like effect, y’know, bars and all that across the back, are particularly striking not to say sticking. The official costume for men, above the waistline, is a more or less fancy-patterned shirt, with or without collar, and a straw hat. . . . We did hear of one party, the ladies gowned in kimonos and the men in rather abbreviated costume, that made a trip in company with a quart brick of ice cream (via automobile) a long way out the St. Marys road. Sounded like a cool party, in fact.”
The article went on to describe the large crowds of “bathers” swimming all along the Avon River in Stratford, attempting to get some respite from the suffocating heat. Another front-page article about the heat wave was published the following day in the Herald, describing locals feeling the heat from the hot pavement permeating through the soles of their shoes, with hot tar from the road adhering to some people’s heels.
One local man, Charles A. Down, reported he was able to fry an egg on the Ontario Street pavement! People were also finding interesting places to sleep, with the upper storeys of homes being much too hot to bear. The newspaper reported people found sleeping on their verandahs, on the roofs of their woodsheds, and even two young men found asleep in a canoe under a willow tree on the Avon River.
Bathing houses, like the one on the Avon River in this photograph from the collections at the Stratford-Perth Archives, reported a record number of swimsuits rented.
Waterworks officials were shocked to find that the water in the city’s storage tank was falling very rapidly, so much so that they sent workers out to find a leak in the mains. After some investigation, it was determined the people of the city were just drinking so much water at once that it drained the tank at a record speed. Families were also finding that the food in their homes was spoiling much faster than usual in the heat.
“The fall wheat, owing to the hot spell, has ripened very rapidly and cutting will commence the latter part of this week. . . . The hot spell has made sleeping upstairs an impossibility and many of our citizens, who are not the happy possessors of sleeping porches, have been making impromptu beds on downstairs floors and on verandahs and piazzas. . . . As between tar and dust on the streets most businessmen and householders would almost prefer the dust. Women complain that their floors have been gummed up and children’s shoes and clothes have been ruined beyond repair. . . . The heat wave that struck Ontario about June 24 has been growing in intensity ever since and, during the past few days, has been well-nigh intolerable. On Sunday and Monday, local thermometers registered over 95 F in the shade. The weatherman, however, has been intimating that relief is in sight.”
And, thankfully relief did come for Perth County residents and the rest of Ontario. But another, much briefer heat wave that arrived during the last few days of August likely terrified Ontarians, thinking they may be in for another few weeks of unbearable temperatures. Luckily, the “hot wave” only lasted around three days before temperatures fell back down below 30 C. However, one journalist lamented about an unpleasant side effect of the hot and balmy weather:
“The hot wave of the past few days has brought the ‘skittas’ (mosquitos) back in full force and the miserable things are going to it as though they hadn’t had anything to eat for a month.”
The 1921 heat wave ended being quite historic for Ontario and the northeastern United States, with long-standing records set that were not broken again for almost a century. Luckily, extreme heat isn’t something we have to worry about right now at this time of year in Ontario and, with any luck, we won’t be breaking cold temperature records this winter season either!

Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH) fell below $2,000 today, for the first time since August, even as staking surged to an all-time high. ETH trades at $1,999 at 10:14 a.m. ET, down 3.6% over the past 24 hours, after dipping as low as $1,981 during the session.
ETH last traded below $2,000 on August 19, when it reached a daily low of $1,905, and it came close again on November 10, hitting a low of $2,003. ETH now trades 59.6% below its all-time high of $4,946, reached on August 24, 2025.
Despite this price decline, more holders are staking their ETH. The staking ratio, which indicates the percentage of all ETH deposited with validators (the computers that help secure the network) to earn rewards, has climbed to 36.3%, according to data from Token Terminal. So why are holders putting more into Ethereum staking even as prices drop?
Why Did ETH Fall Below $2,000?
The market experienced a widespread sell-off that hit every major cryptocurrency. Over the same 24 hours, Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) fell 3.6% to $71,285, while Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) dropped 4.7% to $80.73. For Ethereum, continued selling from fund investors and options dealers’ hedging drove the decline.
On November 11, spot Ethereum ETFs—funds that hold ETH for investors to buy shares via a traditional brokerage—saw net outflows of $145 million. The iShares Ethereum Trust (NASDAQ:ETHA) was responsible for $130 million of that outflow. When investors withdraw money, these ETFs typically sell ETH, increasing market supply.
Options trading has also added to the selling pressure. Coinbase Markets estimated a $589 million short-gamma pocket near $1,980. “Short gamma” refers to how options dealers, who sold those contracts, hedge their positions by selling ETH when prices fall and buying when they rise. This practice can amplify price drops.
ETH hit its session low of $1,981 during the session’s busiest trading hour, right at the edge of that cluster, suggesting dealer hedging added to the sell-off.
Who Is Still Staking ETH?
Staking, which involves locking ETH with a validator to help support the network in exchange for rewards, appeals to long-term holders. Even when prices drop, these holders still earn rewards in additional ETH. Our analysis of whether staking ETH is still worth it compares those rewards with a 10-year Treasury.
Some of the newest stakers are investment funds. The Grayscale Ethereum Staking Mini ETF (NYSEARCA:ETH) stakes the ETH it holds, letting investors collect rewards without running a validator. Funds like Grayscale’s have grown more comfortable staking since the SEC clarified its staking rules.
Treasury firms—public companies that keep cryptocurrency on their balance sheets—are also staking ETH. Bit Digital (NASDAQ:BTBT) reported holding about 163,726 ETH (worth about $327 million) on September 30 and liquid-staked 73,683 ETH during the quarter. Liquid staking provides a tradable receipt token that tracks the staked ETH. However, larger treasury holders face strain, as Bitmine’s paper losses show.
Staked ETH also isn’t easy to sell quickly. A holder who wants out must join the validator exit queue, which grows longer when many people try to leave at once. Therefore, those still staking tend to be long-term holders who are not looking to sell, and their coins can’t re-enter the market quickly even if they change their minds.
Can an All-Time High in Staking Support Ethereum’s Price?
The high staking ratio alone probably won’t stabilize Ethereum’s price unless new buyers emerge. The staking ratio reflects a commitment from current holders, but the coins that still trade set the price. ETH trades below its 20-day average of $2,257, its 50-day average of $2,443, and its 200-day average of $2,151, and being under all three averages indicates that sellers control the market on every time frame.
ETH has also fallen harder than Bitcoin. This week, ETH dropped 8.2%, while Bitcoin fell 3.1% and Solana fell 6.8%. Over the past month, ETH declined 17.8%, against Bitcoin’s 11.4% drop and Solana’s 22.1% fall. We think Bitcoin’s larger base of ETF and corporate buyers explains most of ETH’s sharper decline, as we covered in why Ethereum falls harder than Bitcoin.
Why Are Holders Locking Up More ETH as the Price Falls?
Holders continue to stake their ETH because the rewards keep adding coins, funds can now stake on behalf of investors, and treasury firms are staking their holdings too. The 36.3% staking ratio suggests strong conviction among existing holders. However, for prices to recover, the market needs fresh buyers, and ETF flows are the clearest sign of whether they’re returning.
If spot Ethereum ETFs see net inflows and ETH closes above its 200-day average of $2,151, the drop below $2,000 was probably a short-lived washout. After a daily close below the $1,980 hedging cluster, dealers could add more selling, and our look at how low ETH and Solana could go maps that downside. A longer exit queue during ETF outflows would mean conviction is breaking, turning staked coins into the next wave of supply.

TAX relief measures, particularly the removal of value-added tax (VAT) on system losses and income tax exemptions for low-income earners, received the strongest public support among 10 national issues presented in the latest survey of Publicus Asia.
The scrapping of VAT charges on system losses ranked first, with 80 percent of respondents expressing support, followed by exempting individuals earning less than P350,000 annually from income tax, which received 77-percent support.
The findings of the survey, conducted from Oct. 1 to 4, reflect strong public backing for measures aimed at easing the financial burden on Filipino households, according to Publicus Asia.
Also getting substantial support was the implementation of active shooter drills and other preventive security measures in public and private schools, with 74 percent backing the proposal.
Government transparency and accountability initiatives also figured among the issues presented in the survey, with 61 percent supporting the use of blockchain technology in the national budget under the proposed CADENA Bill.

The proposed ban on social media access for individuals aged 18 and below received 57 percent.
Two issues involving Vice President Sara Duterte and the Senate impeachment court each garnered 48 percent. These were the filing of additional grave-threat charges against Duterte before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court and the Senate impeachment court’s decision to calculate the required two-thirds vote based on senators able to participate in the final vote.
The concerns raised by Caloocan Rep. Edgar Erice over the allocation and use of the Local Government Support Fund received 46 percent.
Rounding out the 10 issues was the government’s response to traffic congestion along the North Luzon Expressway during heavy flooding in Pampanga, which received 44-percent support.
